subject: science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Food chains and the direction of energy flow
Food webs and how they connect organisms
Interdependence and effects of population change
Insect pollination and its importance for food

questions.q: What is a producer in an ecosystem?
options: An animal that hunts other animals
An organism that makes its own food using light in photosynthesis
An organism that eats only dead material
An animal that is eaten by a predator
questions.explain: A producer, usually a green plant, makes its own food from light energy in photosynthesis. It traps the energy that all the consumers in the food chain then depend on.

questions.q: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, which organism is a herbivore (a consumer that eats plants)?
options: Grass
The rabbit
The fox
None of them
questions.explain: The rabbit eats the grass (a plant), so it is a herbivore. The grass is a producer and the fox is a carnivore/predator.

questions.lo: Food chains and the direction of energy flow
questions.q: In a food chain, what does an arrow show?
options: The direction energy flows, from the food to the feeder
Which animal is the strongest
The direction the animals travel
How much the animals weigh
questions.explain: Arrows point in the direction energy flows, from the organism being eaten to the organism doing the eating. They do NOT simply mean 'eats' pointing at the food.

questions.lo: Food chains and the direction of energy flow
questions.q: A student writes the chain 'lettuce → slug → hedgehog'. What does 'slug → hedgehog' tell you?
options: The slug eats the hedgehog
The hedgehog eats the slug and gains its energy
The slug and hedgehog both eat lettuce
The hedgehog is a producer
questions.explain: The arrow runs from the slug to the hedgehog, so energy passes from the slug to the hedgehog — meaning the hedgehog eats the slug.

questions.lo: Food webs and how they connect organisms
options: A single line showing one predator and one prey
A diagram of many food chains joined together, showing how organisms are connected
A list of only the producers in a habitat
A chart of the weather in a habitat
questions.explain: A food web joins many overlapping food chains together. It shows that most organisms eat, and are eaten by, several different species.

questions.lo: Food webs and how they connect organisms
questions.q: In a food web, a mouse is eaten by both an owl and a fox. What does this show?
options: The mouse is a producer
The mouse can be prey to more than one predator
The mouse cannot be eaten
The owl and fox are herbivores
questions.explain: One animal can be prey to several predators. This is why real habitats are drawn as food webs rather than single straight food chains.

questions.lo: Interdependence and effects of population change
questions.q: What does it mean to say organisms in an ecosystem are interdependent?
options: They all live completely separately
They rely on one another for survival, so a change to one affects others
They are all exactly the same species
They never eat each other
questions.explain: Interdependence means organisms depend on each other. Because a food web is so connected, a change in one population can affect many others.

questions.lo: Interdependence and effects of population change
questions.q: In a food web, rabbits eat grass and foxes eat rabbits. If a disease kills most of the rabbits, what is the most likely effect?
options: The number of foxes falls because they have less food
The grass immediately dies out
The foxes turn into producers
Nothing at all changes
questions.explain: Fewer rabbits means less food for the foxes, so fox numbers are likely to fall. With fewer rabbits eating it, the grass would tend to increase, not die out.

questions.lo: Interdependence and effects of population change
questions.q: Why can removing just one species from a food web affect many other species?
options: Because every species is unconnected to the others
Because organisms are linked through feeding relationships, so a change spreads through the web
Because all species eat exactly the same food
Because species always move away when one is removed
questions.explain: Species are joined through many feeding links. Removing one changes the numbers of the things that ate it and the things it ate, and those changes ripple on to others.

questions.q: On a predator–prey graph, which population usually reaches its peak first?
options: The predator
The prey
They always peak at the same time
Neither ever changes
questions.explain: The prey peak comes first. More prey means more food for predators, so the predator population grows and peaks a little afterwards.

questions.q: The number of foxes in a woodland rises. What is the most likely effect on the rabbit population they hunt?
options: Rabbit numbers rise because there are more foxes
Rabbit numbers fall because more rabbits are eaten
Rabbit numbers stay exactly the same forever
The rabbits turn into predators
questions.explain: More predators eat more prey, so the rabbit (prey) population tends to fall. Later, with less food, the fox numbers drop and the rabbits can recover — a repeating cycle.

questions.q: Why do organisms in a habitat compete?
options: Because resources are limited and there is not enough for all
Because they enjoy fighting
Because resources are unlimited
Because they all belong to the same species
questions.explain: Resources such as food, water, light and space are limited, so organisms compete for whatever there is not enough of.

questions.q: Two plants grow very close together in a garden. Which of these are they most likely to compete for?
options: Prey and mates
Light, water, space and soil minerals
Somewhere to hide from predators
Nothing, because plants never compete
questions.explain: Plants compete for light (for photosynthesis), water, space and minerals from the soil. They do not hunt prey or need mates in the way animals do.

options: Toxic materials being broken down and removed by animals
Toxic materials building up in organisms and increasing along a food chain
Plants making their own food from light
Animals competing for water
questions.explain: Bioaccumulation is when a toxic material that cannot be broken down builds up in organisms. Its concentration increases at each step up the food chain.

questions.q: A pesticide that cannot be broken down leaks into a lake with the chain: plankton → small fish → big fish → heron. Which organism ends up with the highest concentration of the pesticide?
options: The plankton
The small fish
The heron
They all have the same amount
questions.explain: The toxin builds up at each stage, so the top predator — the heron — ends up with the highest concentration, even if the amount in the water is small.

questions.q: Why can a toxic material harm top predators even when only a tiny amount is in the environment?
options: Because top predators drink the most water
Because the toxin is concentrated as it is passed up each level of the food chain
Because top predators make their own toxins
Because the toxin only affects producers
questions.explain: The toxin passes from prey to predator and cannot be removed, so it becomes more concentrated at each level. Top predators eat many contaminated animals, so they collect the most.

questions.lo: Insect pollination and its importance for food
options: The transfer of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part
A plant eating an insect
The building up of toxins in a food chain
An animal competing for a mate
questions.explain: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the female part of a flower, which allows the plant to make seeds and fruit. Many plants rely on insects to carry the pollen.

questions.lo: Insect pollination and its importance for food
questions.q: Why would a large fall in the number of insect pollinators, such as bees, be a serious problem for human food supplies?
options: Bees are the main food eaten by humans
Many food crops need insect pollination to make fruit and seeds, so yields would fall
Bees are producers that make all our oxygen
Bees break down the toxins in food chains
questions.explain: A large share of crops (such as apples, strawberries and beans) depend on insect pollination to set fruit and seeds. Fewer pollinators means smaller harvests and less food for people.

specSource: National Curriculum in England: science programme of study, Key Stage 3; Biology — Interactions and interdependencies
